replacement: “You must tell me all that afterwards, afterwards!” Madame Hohlakov raised her hand and demanded silence in her turn. “And whatever you tell me, I know it all beforehand. I’ve said so already. You ask for a certain sum, three thousand, but I can give you more, immeasurably more. I will save you, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, but you must listen to me.”
“You’re lying!” shouted Mitya. “From your terror I know where she is.”

He rushed off. Fenya, in her fright, was glad to have got away so lightly. But she knew very well that he had only been in too much of a hurry, or she might not have fared so well. And as he ran, he startled both Fenya and old Matryona with something unexpected. On the table stood a brass mortar with a pestle in it, a small brass pestle, hardly more than six inches long. Mitya already had the door open with one hand when, with the other, he grabbed the pestle and shoved it into his side pocket.

He settled on a different plan. He went a long way around Fyodor Pavlovitch’s house, crossed the lane, ran down Dmitrovsky Street and over the little bridge, and came out at the deserted alley behind the house, which was empty and uninhabited. On one side was the wattle fence of a neighbor’s kitchen-garden. On the other was the tall, strong fence that ran all around Fyodor Pavlovitch’s garden. Here he chose a spot, apparently the very one where, as the story went and he knew it, Lizaveta had once climbed over. “If she could climb over it,” the thought came to him, God knows why, “surely I can.” He jumped up and at once got a grip on the top of the fence. Then he hauled himself up with all his strength and sat astride it. The bath-house stood close by in the garden, but from the fence he could also see the lit windows of the house.
